title: Fine-tuning LLMs
summary: Fine-tuning adapts a pretrained model to your specific data or style. You format examples, run supervised training with the Hugging Face Trainer, and evaluate the results. Even small fine-tunes can dramatically improve performance on niche tasks, a h
content:
# Fine-tuning LLMs ##### The model that learned to apologise A fintech in Mumbai wanted their support assistant to write in the company's voice: short, direct, no filler, always ending with a concrete next step. Prompting got them 70% of the way — but the stock model kept producing "I'm so sorry to hear about your frustrating experience!" openers that their brand team hated, and every fourth response drifted back into corporate padding no matter how firmly the system prompt objected. They collected 800 real support replies written by their best three agents, formatted them as instruction-response pairs, and fine-tuned a small model for forty minutes. The apologising stopped. Completely. Response length dropped from an average of 140 words to 52. The brand team approved it on the first review. **This is what fine-tuning is genuinely good at.** Not adding knowledge — Day 27 was emphatic about that — but locking in a *behaviour* that prompting can only approximate. When you need something to happen 100% of the time rather than 70%, and you can demonstrate it with examples, fine-tuning is the tool. Today you do it end to end. ##### When you have arrived at fine-tuning Before writing any code, confirm you are here for the right reason: - ✅ You need a consistent **format** (always valid JSON matching a schema). - ✅ You need a specific **tone or style**. - ✅ You have a **narrow task** the model does clumsily. - ✅ You want a **small model to match a large one** on one job, for cost and latency. - ❌ You need the model to know facts → **RAG**. - ❌ You have not seriously tried prompting → **do that first**. - ❌ You have 40 examples → **collect more, use few-shot meanwhile**. The rough data requirement: **500 examples minimum, 1,000–10,000 for good results.** Quality matters far more than quantity. Two hundred excellent, consistent examples beat five thousand noisy ones — and inconsistency in your training data teaches the model to be inconsistent. ##### Dataset formatting Your data becomes a text file where each example demonstrates the behaviour. The format depends on the model. **Causal LM (GPT-style) — the completion format:** ```python import json examples = [ {"instruction": "A customer says their UPI payment was debited but the order " "did not confirm. Write a support reply.", "response": "Your payment is being verified with the bank. If the order does " "not confirm within 2 hours, the amount auto-refunds in 3-5 " "working days. Reference: TXN-88231. Reply here if it does not."}, {"instruction": "A customer asks how to update the GSTIN on their invoice.", "response": "Go to Settings > Billing > Tax Details and update your GSTIN. " "Invoices from the next cycle will reflect it. For a past invoice, " "raise a reissue request from the same page."}, ] with open("data/train.jsonl", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f: for ex in examples: f.write(json.dumps(ex, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n") ``` **Chat format**, for instruct models: ```python {"messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a concise support agent. No apologies. " "Always end with a next step."}, {"role": "user", "content": "My UPI payment was debited but no order."}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "Your payment is being verified..."} ]} ``` **Three formatting rules that determine whether this works:** 1. **Be consistent.** Every example uses the same structure, the same separators, the same style. The model learns the pattern you repeat — including accidental ones. 2. **Mask the prompt in the loss.** You want the model to learn to produce *responses*, not to reproduce instructions. Set instruction-token labels to `-100` so they are excluded from the loss. 3. **Include an EOS token.** Without it the model never learns to stop, and generation runs until it hits the token limit — a very common and very confusing first-fine-tune bug. ```python from transformers import AutoTokenizer from datasets import load_dataset MODEL = "distilgpt2" tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL) tokenizer.pad_token = tokenizer.eos_token # GPT-2 has no pad token PROMPT_TEMPLATE = "### Instruction:\n{instruction}\n\n### Response:\n" def format_and_tokenize(example, max_length=512): prompt = PROMPT_TEMPLATE.format(instruction=example["instruction"]) full = prompt + example["response"] + tokenizer.eos_token tokenized = tokenizer(full, truncation=True, max_length=max_length, padding="max_length") prompt_len = len(tokenizer(prompt, truncation=True, max_length=max_length)["input_ids"]) labels = tokenized["input_ids"].copy() labels[:prompt_len] = [-100] * prompt_len # mask the prompt labels = [-100 if t == tokenizer.pad_token_id else l for t, l in zip(tokenized["input_ids"], labels)] # mask padding tokenized["labels"] = labels return tokenized raw = load_dataset("json", data_files={"train": "data/train.jsonl"})["train"] split = raw.train_test_split(test_size=0.1, seed=42) tokenized = split.map(format_and_tokenize, remove_columns=split["train"].column_names) ``` The `-100` value is PyTorch's ignore index for cross-entropy — those positions contribute nothing to the loss. ##### Supervised fine-tuning with Trainer ```python import torch from transformers import (AutoModelForCausalLM, TrainingArguments, Trainer, DataCollatorForLanguageModeling, EarlyStoppingCallback) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(MODEL) model.resize_token_embeddings(len(tokenizer)) args = TrainingArguments( output_dir="./sft-support-agent", # --- the parameters that matter most --- learning_rate=2e-5, # LOW. 1e-5 to 5e-5 for fine-tuning. num_train_epochs=3, # 2-4. More overfits fast. per_device_train_batch_size=4, gradient_accumulation_steps=4, # effective batch = 4 × 4 = 16 warmup_ratio=0.06, weight_decay=0.01, lr_scheduler_type="cosine", max_grad_norm=1.0, # gradient clipping # --- evaluation and checkpointing --- eval_strategy="epoch", save_strategy="epoch", save_total_limit=2, load_best_model_at_end=True, metric_for_best_model="eval_loss", greater_is_better=False, # --- efficiency --- fp16=torch.cuda.is_available(), gradient_checkpointing=True, # trades compute for memory logging_steps=25, report_to="none", seed=42, ) trainer = Trainer( model=model, args=args, train_dataset=tokenized["train"], eval_dataset=tokenized["test"], data_collator=DataCollatorForLanguageModeling(tokenizer, mlm=False), callbacks=[EarlyStoppingCallback(early_stopping_patience=2)], ) trainer.train() trainer.save_model("./sft-support-agent/final") tokenizer.save_pretrained("./sft-support-agent/final") ``` **The three settings people get wrong:** - **Learning rate.** 2e-5 is a sensible default. Use 1e-3 and you will destroy the pretrained weights in the first hundred steps — catastrophic forgetting, the same principle as Day 17's transfer learning. - **Epochs.** Two to four. LLM fine-tuning overfits remarkably fast on small datasets; by epoch six the model is often reciting training examples verbatim. - **Gradient accumulation.** When your GPU cannot hold a batch of 16, run four batches of 4 and accumulate gradients before stepping. Mathematically almost identical, memory-wise very different. `gradient_checkpointing=True` recomputes activations during the backward pass instead of storing them — roughly 30% slower, but it can halve memory usage. On a free Colab T4 it is often the difference between running and not running. ##### Evaluating generations This is where fine-tuning differs hardest from classification. There is no accuracy score for "did it write in our voice." **Validation loss** is your first signal, and it tells you about fit, not quality: ```python import math metrics = trainer.evaluate() print(f"eval loss: {metrics['eval_loss']:.4f}") print(f"perplexity: {math.exp(metrics['eval_loss']):.2f}") ``` Perplexity is `exp(loss)` — roughly, how many tokens the model is choosing between at each step. Lower is better, but a low perplexity model can still produce output you hate. **Before/after comparison** is the honest evaluation, and it is non-negotiable: ```python import torch def generate(model, tokenizer, instruction, max_new_tokens=120): prompt = PROMPT_TEMPLATE.format(instruction=instruction) inputs = tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt").to(model.device) model.eval() with torch.no_grad(): out = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens=max_new_tokens, do_sample=True, temperature=0.7, top_p=0.9, repetition_penalty=1.1, pad_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id, eos_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id, ) return tokenizer.decode(out[0][inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:], skip_special_tokens=True) base = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(MODEL) tuned = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("./sft-support-agent/final") held_out = [ "A customer's refund has not arrived after 8 working days.", "A customer asks whether you deliver to Port Blair.", ] for q in held_out: print("=" * 70) print("Q: ", q) print("BASE: ", generate(base, tokenizer, q)) print("TUNED: ", generate(tuned, tokenizer, q)) ``` **Then evaluate systematically.** Define 3–5 criteria and score 30–50 held-out generations against them: | Criterion | How to measure | |---|---| | Format compliance | Regex / JSON parse — automatable | | Length | Token count within target range | | Tone | Human rating 1–5, or LLM-as-judge | | Factual correctness | Human check against source | | Refusal to hallucinate | Include unanswerable questions and check | **Automated metrics with real caveats:** BLEU and ROUGE measure n-gram overlap with a reference and are weak proxies for quality — a perfectly good paraphrase scores badly. BERTScore is better. **LLM-as-judge** — asking a strong model to rate outputs against a rubric — correlates reasonably well with human judgement and scales, but has known biases toward longer responses and toward its own outputs. For the Mumbai team, the evaluation that mattered was mechanical: *does the response contain an apology phrase, and is it under 80 words?* Two regexes. 96% pass rate after fine-tuning versus 31% before. ##### The training loop, visualised ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Collect 500-10,000
high-quality examples"] --> B["Format consistently
+ mask prompt tokens"] B --> C["Split: 90% train / 10% eval"] C --> D["Generate BASELINE outputs
on held-out set"] D --> E["Train: lr 2e-5, 2-4 epochs"] E --> F{"eval_loss
improving?"} F -->|Rising| G["Overfitting:
stop early, fewer epochs,
more data"] F -->|Flat| H["Underfitting:
higher lr, more epochs"] F -->|Falling| I["Generate TUNED outputs
on same held-out set"] I --> J["Score both against
your criteria"] J --> K{"Better?"} K -->|Yes| L["Ship"] K -->|No| M["Fix the DATA,
not the hyperparameters"] M --> A ``` That last arrow is the one beginners resist. When a fine-tune disappoints, the instinct is to tune the learning rate. **The problem is almost always the data** — inconsistent examples, too few, or demonstrating a behaviour subtly different from what you wanted. ##### Common pitfalls - **Learning rate too high** — the model forgets how to speak English. Symptom: fluent gibberish. - **Too many epochs** — the model recites training examples verbatim. Symptom: eval loss rising while train loss falls. - **No EOS token** in training data — generation never stops. - **Not masking prompt tokens**, so the model learns to reproduce instructions. - **Inconsistent formatting** across examples, teaching inconsistency. - **No held-out set**, so you have no idea whether it helped. - **No before/after comparison** — the only evaluation that actually convinces anyone. - **Fine-tuning for knowledge** instead of behaviour. - **Forgetting `tokenizer.pad_token = tokenizer.eos_token`** for GPT-2 family models. - **Full fine-tuning on a 7B model** when LoRA would use 1% of the memory — tomorrow's topic. - **Not saving the tokenizer** alongside the model, making the checkpoint unloadable. - **Testing only on training-like inputs** and missing that the model got worse at everything else. ##### Hands-on: run one end to end Your practical task is fine-tuning DistilGPT-2 on a small custom dataset with before/after samples. DistilGPT-2 is only 82M parameters, so it trains on a free Colab T4 in minutes and even on CPU in a reasonable time. Pick a dataset with a strong, obvious style — recipes, haikus, git commit messages, Shakespeare dialogue — because with a small model and a small dataset you need the signal to be loud enough to see. Generate five samples before training and the same five after, and put them side by side. The mini project fine-tunes a model to answer in a specific tone or domain and demonstrates the improvement. The demonstration is the deliverable, not the training. Define your success criteria *before* you train — write down the three things you will check — then measure both models against them and report the numbers. "Format compliance went from 31% to 96% on 50 held-out prompts" is a result. "It seems better" is not. The assignment documents a full experiment: dataset prep, config, metrics, lessons. Include your failures. The run where you used lr=1e-3 and got gibberish teaches more than the successful one, and writing up "here is what catastrophic forgetting actually looked like" demonstrates real understanding. Log everything — dataset size, hyperparameters, loss curves, sample outputs — so the experiment is reproducible. ##### Key takeaways - **Fine-tune for behaviour, not knowledge**: consistent format, specific tone, a narrow task — the things prompting gets to 70% and you need at 100%. - **Data quality dominates.** 500 consistent examples beat 5,000 noisy ones, and when a fine-tune disappoints the fix is almost always the data, not the hyperparameters. - **Mask prompt tokens with `-100` and include an EOS token** — these two details cause most first-fine-tune failures. - **Use lr 1e-5 to 5e-5 for 2–4 epochs.** Higher destroys pretrained weights; longer overfits and produces verbatim recitation. - **Always generate before/after on a held-out set** and score against criteria you defined in advance — validation loss tells you about fit, not about whether the output is good.
